History

The recycler bong is a recent design, developed in the 2010s as glassblowers working on concentrate rigs looked for a way to keep water moving instead of letting it sit still. The idea borrows from the Klein bottle, a mathematical shape with no inside or outside, and some recycler designs are still called Klein recyclers for the sealed loop their glass forms. Early recyclers were small dab rigs; the loop layout then spread to flower bongs, with two chambers joined by an uptake tube and a drain tube so water circulates while smoke travels to the mouthpiece. Trade guides describe the loop as doing three jobs at once: it keeps the percolator covered, it keeps water off the user's lips, and it keeps smoke bubbles surrounded by water longer. The design is now a recognised type in its own right, sold alongside beakers and straight tubes. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Trade guides and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The recycler bong works by smoke and water circulate together in a loop: the percolator diffuses smoke in the main chamber, an uptake tube carries water and smoke up to a second chamber where they separate, and a drain tube returns the water to the main chamber. It is made from borosilicate glass main chamber, secondary chamber, uptake tube and drain tube, showerhead percolator, glass downstem and bowl, water as the filtration and circulation medium, and a common example measures 340 mm tall, main chamber 300 ml, secondary chamber 150 ml, uptake tube 10 mm diameter, drain tube 8 mm diameter, water 180 ml in total. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Borosilicate glass main chamber, secondary chamber, uptake tube, and drain tube; showerhead percolator; glass downstem and bowl; plain water as the filtration and circulation medium

Dimensions: 340 mm tall; main chamber 300 mL; secondary chamber 150 mL; uptake tube 10 mm diameter; drain tube 8 mm diameter; water 180 mL in total

Mechanism: The percolator diffuses smoke in the main chamber; the draw pulls water and smoke up the uptake tube into the secondary chamber, where water and smoke separate; gravity drains the water back through the drain tube to the main chamber, and the loop repeats while the draw continues

Use: Add water so the percolator is covered but the upper chamber stays dry when still, pack the bowl, draw steadily so the loop starts, then clear

Care: Change the water after each session; soak the loop tubes in isopropyl alcohol; rinse well; dry fully; handle gently because the loop tubes are thin

Variants: External recycler with visible parallel tubes; internal recycler with hidden tubes; Klein recycler with a sealed loop; double showerhead recycler

Materials and design

Borosilicate glass is chosen for the recycler because the loop is made of thin tubes fused at several joints, and only a glass that tolerates heat and holds a fine fused joint will keep those tubes from cracking where they meet the chambers. The uptake tube is wider than the drain tube because it carries a two-phase flow, water and smoke together, while the drain carries water alone, and a tube that is too narrow for its flow will choke and break the loop. The joints are the same ground-glass tapers as on the beaker, 14 mm or 18 mm, sealing by friction with no gasket and no thread. The outside is left smooth and clear so the circulating water can be seen, which is part of the appeal of the design and the easiest way to check that the loop is running.

Build it yourself

A recycler bong cannot be made at home: fusing a loop of uptake and drain tubes between two glass chambers is a skilled glassblowing trade, and no home method produces it safely. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling a bought kit and making a padded carry cradle for it. Buy a recycler body, a downstem, and a bowl in matching joint sizes, and check the fit dry before any water goes in: the downstem should seat firmly without wobble, and the water must cover the percolator while leaving the upper chamber dry when still. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, and work slowly, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

3D printing

A glass recycler bong is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic loop could not hold the fused uptake and drain tubes or seal to a glass downstem. Print time (estimate): 2 hours 30 minutes for the cradle and 1 hour 15 minutes for the guard, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing, and the estimate above is not a validated print job.

Use and program

Add water so the percolator is covered but the upper chamber stays dry when the piece is still, checking the level by eye before the first draw. Pack the bowl loosely and draw steadily: within the first second the water should start moving up the uptake tube, and the loop should keep running for as long as the draw continues. Then lift the bowl and inhale to clear. The program in this record computes the uptake and drain tube cross-sections, the loop water volume, and the loop time from the loop volume divided by the draw flow rate, so the user can check that the loop is sized to keep the percolator covered for the whole pull. Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.
build_yourself: This section gives the closest genuine maker activity for this supply, honestly labelled. A recycler bong cannot be made at home: fusing a loop of uptake and drain tubes between two glass chambers is a skilled glassblowing trade, and no home method produces it safely. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling a bought kit and making a padded carry cradle for it. Buy a recycler body, a downstem, and a bowl in matching joint sizes, and check the fit dry before any water goes in: the downstem should seat firmly without wobble, and the water must cover the percolator while leaving the upper chamber dry when still. Then make a cradle from a block of dense foam: trace the recycler's outline on the foam, cut the recess with a sharp knife in shallow passes, and test the fit with the dry piece until it sits without rocking. The cradle protects the thin loop tubes in storage and in transport. Test it by tipping the cradle gently from side to side; the piece should stay seated. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, work slowly, and keep the finished piece clean and dry in storage, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

demo.code:
"""Demo: recycler bong loop volumes and cycle time — The Recycler Bong."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    main_mL = 120.0; sec_mL = 60.0; up_d = 10.0; dr_d = 8.0; up_len = 180.0; dr_len = 150.0; draw = 1.2
    up_area = math.pi * (up_d / 2.0) ** 2
    dr_area = math.pi * (dr_d / 2.0) ** 2
    loop_mL = main_mL + sec_mL
    flow_mL_s = draw * 1000.0 / 60.0
    loop_time = loop_mL / flow_mL_s
    up_vol = up_area * up_len / 1000.0
    return {"main_water_mL": main_mL, "secondary_water_mL": sec_mL, "loop_water_mL": round(loop_mL, 2), "uptake_area_mm2": round(up_area, 2), "drain_area_mm2": round(dr_area, 2), "loop_time_s": round(loop_time, 2), "uptake_volume_mL": round(up_vol, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["main_water_mL", "secondary_water_mL", "loop_water_mL", "uptake_area_mm2", "drain_area_mm2", "loop_time_s", "uptake_volume_mL"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

materials_design: Borosilicate glass is chosen for the recycler because the loop is made of thin tubes fused at several joints, and only a glass that tolerates heat and holds a fine fused joint will keep those tubes from cracking where they meet the chambers. The uptake tube is wider than the drain tube because it carries a two-phase flow, water and smoke together, while the drain carries water alone, and a tube that is too narrow for its flow will choke and break the loop. Water is both the filtration medium and the working fluid of the loop: it must be deep enough to cover the percolator and shallow enough that the upper chamber stays dry when the piece is still. The joints are the same ground-glass tapers as on the beaker, 14 mm or 18 mm, sealing by friction with no gasket and no thread. The loop tubes themselves have no joints: they are fused to the chambers while the glass is hot, so the main chamber, the uptake tube, the secondary chamber, and the drain tube are one continuous piece of glass. The tolerance that matters is the height of the drain outlet in the secondary chamber: if it is too high, water pools in the upper chamber, and if it is too low, the loop drains before it starts. The downstem seats into the main chamber joint at about 45 degrees. The outside is left smooth and clear so the circulating water can be seen, which is part of the appeal of the design and the easiest way to check that the loop is running. The fused joints are annealed slowly so they do not hold stress. Variants change whether the loop tubes run outside the body where they can be seen or inside it where they are protected, and whether the loop is a plain circuit or a Klein-style sealed loop, but the two chambers and the two tubes stay the same in every version.
math_proof: The demo starts from the tube cross-sections: the uptake tube has a diameter of 10.0 mm, so its area is pi times its radius squared, and the drain tube has a diameter of 8.0 mm, with its area computed the same way. The loop water volume is the main chamber water of 120.0 mL plus the secondary chamber water of 60.0 mL. The draw flow rate is 1.2 litres per minute, which divided by 60 gives millilitres per second, and dividing the loop volume by that flow gives the loop time in seconds. The uptake tube volume is its cross-section times its length of 180.0 mm, reported in millilitres. All numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each result with its unit so the reader can repeat the arithmetic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation. The computation is run twice and the SHA-256 digests of both runs are printed, confirming the result is deterministic.
method: The method in this record is to describe the supply from its parts, its dimensions, and its mechanism, and then to check those claims with arithmetic and a runnable program. First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. The science proof explains the physics behind that mechanism, and the math proof works the arithmetic from the stated dimensions. Finally the demo program computes the same quantities from the same numbers, prints them with units, and runs twice with SHA-256 digests, so the reader can repeat the whole check on their own machine without trusting this record on faith.
print3d: Home 3D printing cannot make every supply in this database, and this section says plainly where the limit falls. A glass recycler bong is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic loop could not hold the fused uptake and drain tubes or seal to a glass downstem. The printable accessory is a protective carry cradle and a loop-tube guard for the piece. Print the cradle in TPU, which stays flexible and grips the glass without scratching it, with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, 3 perimeters, and 20 percent gyroid infill, and print the guard in PETG with the same nozzle and layer height at 25 percent infill. Print the cradle flat on its bottom face with no supports, and the guard upright with a brim. Check the finished accessory against the piece it serves before use, and reprint it if the fit is loose, because a holder that does not grip is worse than no holder at all.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: recycler bong needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.

"""The Recycler Bong — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (recycler bong loop volumes and cycle time),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for The Recycler Bong."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        main_mL = 120.0; sec_mL = 60.0; up_d = 10.0; dr_d = 8.0; up_len = 180.0; dr_len = 150.0; draw = 1.2
        up_area = math.pi * (up_d / 2.0) ** 2
        dr_area = math.pi * (dr_d / 2.0) ** 2
        loop_mL = main_mL + sec_mL
        flow_mL_s = draw * 1000.0 / 60.0
        loop_time = loop_mL / flow_mL_s
        up_vol = up_area * up_len / 1000.0
        return {"main_water_mL": main_mL, "secondary_water_mL": sec_mL, "loop_water_mL": round(loop_mL, 2), "uptake_area_mm2": round(up_area, 2), "drain_area_mm2": round(dr_area, 2), "loop_time_s": round(loop_time, 2), "uptake_volume_mL": round(up_vol, 2)}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

science_proof: The recycler works by keeping water in motion. In a plain bong the water sits still and the smoke passes through it once; in a recycler the draw creates a pressure difference that pulls water up the uptake tube into the secondary chamber, where the water and the smoke separate because water is far denser than smoke and falls back under gravity. The drain tube carries that water back to the main chamber, so the percolator never runs dry during a long pull, which is the failure that makes a plain percolator gurgle and splash. The loop time is the loop water volume divided by the draw flow rate: at a draw of 1.2 litres per minute the 180 millilitres of water in the loop takes about nine seconds to make one full circuit. The uptake tube must be wider than the drain tube, because it carries water and smoke together while the drain carries water alone, and a drain that is too narrow will back up and flood the upper chamber. The smoke is not filtered a second time by the loop: the loop's jobs are to keep the percolator covered, to keep water off the lips, and to keep each bubble surrounded by water longer, which is where the extra cooling comes from. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this record does not prove. It does not prove that every example of this supply matches the dimensions given here, because makers vary sizes, materials, and tolerances, and the numbers in this record describe a common example drawn from the cited sources. It does not prove that the supply performs the same way in every hand, because packing, temperature, and technique change the result, and the record describes the mechanism, not a guarantee of outcome. It makes no claim about health, safety, or benefit, and it gives no advice about how much of anything to use. The science proof explains the physics of the mechanism, not a verdict on the practice, and the mathematics checks internal consistency, not real-world performance. Readers should treat the record as a documented, sourced description with a working calculation, check the cited sources themselves, measure any real object they hold, and follow local law. That is the honest limit of what a reference record can claim.
